name: Cocos Island National Park
blurb: Remote island rainforest and a sea of hammerheads, tuna and seabirds.

tip.title: Thin out the flying fish
tip.text: Flying fish feed boobies, frigatebirds, tuna and dolphins. Set Flying fish to -100% and watch the seabirds and tuna, then the hammerheads and false killer whales above them.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage: Cocos Island National Park

notes: The species list comes from GBIF occurrence records inside a circle around the park, so it can include nearby areas. Feeding links come from GloBI records and the sources listed where they state them; others are general ecology and are illustrative.

nodes.desc: Powers the algae of the sunlit sea and the dense forest canopy of the island.
Fungi, bacteria and insects break down dead leaves, wood and carcasses, returning nutrients to the thin acidic island soil.
Microscopic algae in the sunlit water around the island, the base of the open-ocean food chain.
A genus of berry-bearing shrubs and small trees. Miconia are among the most recorded plants in the cloud forest, which is dominated by Melastomataceae.
Coastal forest is dominated partly by coconut palm, along with purple coral tree and pond apple.

nodes.name: Copepods
nodes.desc: Tiny crustaceans that graze phytoplankton in the plankton-rich waters of the island, food for fish and whale sharks.
Plankton-feeding fish that leap from the water to escape predators. A staple prey of boobies, frigatebirds and tuna.
Introduced by people; the island has no native land mammals. Deer browse native plants and are a management concern.
Introduced pigs root through the forest and damage native plants and animals; control efforts continue.
An introduced omnivore on the island, listed among the invasive species that harm native wildlife.
Nests in large colonies on the island, often in trees. Plunge-dives for flying fish and squid far out to sea.
Snatches flying fish from the sea surface and often follows tuna or dolphins that drive fish up. Also takes chicks of other seabirds.

nodes.name: Bottlenose dolphin
nodes.desc: A frequently recorded marine mammal around the island, hunting fish and squid in open water.
Gathers around the island by day and hunts offshore at night, mainly bony fish and squid. Endangered, with near-pristine shark numbers here.
